verses.commentary: A prophecy (massa, burden) concerning Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. Nineveh, capital of Assyria, faces judgment. Unlike Jonah's Nineveh that repented, this Nineveh meets doom. About 150 years separate the two prophets.

Triple emphasis: jealous, avenging, wrathful. God takes vengeance on foes and maintains wrath against enemies. Divine jealousy protects covenant relationship. What threatens God's people meets divine resistance.

Slow to anger but great in power. The classic confession from Exodus 34:6 modified. Patience does not mean indifference. The guilty will not go unpunished. Whirlwind and storm are his path; clouds are dust beneath his feet. Theophany language: God approaches.
He rebukes sea, dries rivers. Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon (symbols of fertility and strength) wither. The most verdant regions fade before divine approach. Nature submits to its Creator.
Mountains quake, hills melt. Earth trembles at his presence. World and inhabitants shake. Cosmic response to divine arrival. Creation recognizes its Maker when he moves.

Who can stand against his indignation? Who can endure his anger? Questions without answers. Wrath poured out like fire, rocks shattered. No resistance possible. The rhetorical questions silence all pretension.
The Lord is good. Refuge in trouble. He knows those who trust him. Amid descriptions of terrifying power, comfort emerges. The same God who destroys enemies shelters his own. Two sides of one love.
With overwhelming flood he ends Nineveh. Historically accurate: the Khosr River flooded and breached Nineveh's walls in 612 BC. Pursuing foes into darkness. No escape from divine judgment.
Whatever plots against the Lord, he brings to an end. Conspiracy fails. Trouble will not rise twice (or: a second time). Complete destruction. No need for repeat judgment.

Entangled like thorns, drunk with wine, consumed like dry stubble. Three images of vulnerability. Thorns catch fire easily. Drunkards cannot defend themselves. Stubble burns in moments. Assyria's seeming strength is weakness.

From Nineveh came one who plots evil against the Lord. Likely refers to Sennacherib who blasphemed Yahweh during his invasion of Judah (2 Kings 18-19). Wicked plans (belial, worthlessness) characterized Assyrian policy.

Despite allies and numbers, they will be cut off. God addresses Judah directly: I have afflicted you, but will do so no more. The instrument of discipline (Assyria) now faces judgment. Judah's suffering ends.

Now I break their yoke from your neck, tear your shackles away. Liberation announced. The oppressor becomes the oppressed. Judah's bondage to Assyria concludes. Divine intervention reverses power relations.

Command concerning Nineveh: no descendants to bear your name. Idols and images destroyed in their temples. Grave prepared because they are vile. Dynasty ends, religion ends, existence ends. Total annihilation decreed.

Look on the mountains! Feet of one bringing good news, proclaiming peace! Isaiah 52:7 echoed. Nineveh's fall means Judah's deliverance. Celebrate festivals, fulfill vows. The wicked will never again invade. Complete destruction. Good news arrives because judgment falls on evil.
